stem: Sarah is an 18-month-old with a 2-day history of fever to 39°C and no localising symptoms. She attends day care and has a normal examination apart from fever. Which ONE of the following is the most appropriate method for urine collection in this child?
explanation: In a toilet-trained or young child who is not yet toilet-trained but can void, a clean-catch urine sample is the preferred non-invasive method for urine collection when assessing possible UTI. Bag urine is not suitable for diagnosis because of contamination. Catheterisation or suprapubic aspirate are reserved when a clean catch cannot be obtained or a sterile specimen is specifically required.
rationale: The child is 18 months old with fever without source, so urine testing is indicated. Clean catch is the best available non-invasive collection method in this age group.

optionExplanations.A: Preferred non-invasive method for urine collection in a young child.
optionExplanations.B: More invasive; used if a reliable non-invasive sample cannot be obtained.
optionExplanations.C: Sterile sample method, usually reserved for when catheter/clean catch is not possible.
optionExplanations.D: Typically used in older toilet-trained children, not an 18-month-old.
optionExplanations.E: High contamination risk; not appropriate for diagnosing UTI.

Instructions

There are 7 questions relating to this scenario.

Clinical scenario 2 - Sarah

Sarah, an 18 month old, presents with a two day history of fever to 39°C. She has no history of cough; rhinorrhoea; vomiting; diarrhoea or rash. She attends day care. She has a 5 year old sibling who is at school and is well at the moment. She is eating less than normal but drinking well and passing urine as normal.

On examination she appears slightly flushed with a fever of 38.5°C. Her HR is 110 and RR 28. Her peripheries are warm and her capillary refill time is 1-2 seconds.

She has no rash, no conjunctivitis, her ENT examination is unremarkable. Her heart sounds are dual with no murmur and her chest is clear. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Her immunisations are up to date.

The following seven questions refer to Sarah’s clinical scenario.
